concept.name: Box spread
concept.definition: A box spread is a four-leg, same-expiration position combining a bull call spread and a bear put spread at the same two strikes — equivalently, long call + short put at the lower strike and short call + long put at the upper strike. Constructed with European-style options it has a constant expiration payoff equal to the strike difference, making it a synthetic zero-coupon loan.
concept.intuition: A box is options-market lending: you pay a fixed price today for a guaranteed fixed payoff at expiration, so the only real variable is the implied interest rate.
concept.mechanics: Because the payoff is fixed at (K2 - K1), the fair price is the present value of that amount; paying less is effectively borrowing, paying more is effectively lending at the implied rate. With American-style index or equity options, early exercise of an ITM leg can break the box and convert it into directional exposure — the source of notorious catastrophic retail losses.
concept.formula: Payoff at expiration (long box) = K2 - K1, constant; fair value = (K2 - K1) * e^(-rT) under put-call parity.
concept.failure_modes: Early assignment on American-style legs destroys the fixed payoff and can produce losses vastly larger than the intended interest-like economics (the infamous 1R0NYMAN case, roughly a 2,000% loss on margin). Execution across four legs also invites slippage that erases the thin rate edge.
concept.misconceptions: A box spread is not 'free money' or riskless yield: with American options it embeds assignment tail risk, and the implied rate is only fair compensation for funding, not an arbitrage gift, once costs are included.
concept.example: A 40-50 box (long 40 call, short 50 call, long 50 put, short 40 put) always pays exactly $10 at expiration; paying $9.80 for it today implies earning roughly the risk-free rate to expiry — unless an American-style leg is assigned early.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
